A_target.statement:
Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R_{\ge 0}$ be [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]].
Then the [[Definition:Area|area]] under the graph of $f$ is:
:$\displaystyle \lim_{\norm P \mathop \to 0} \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {x_i^*} \Delta x_i = \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$

B_source.statement:
The total area of finitely many non-overlapping [[Definition:Rectangle|rectangles]] of widths $w_i$ and heights $h_i$ is:
:$\displaystyle \sum_i w_i h_i$

object_map.reformulation: Approximate the region under the curve by thin rectangles, then take the mesh to zero.

validity_conditions: f continuous on [a,b], hence Riemann integrable, so the limit of Riemann sums exists and is independent of the sample points.
The finite rectangle-area formula is exact at each mesh; only the passage to the limit introduces the continuous object.
proof_plan: Let $P = \set {a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b}$ and build rectangles of width $\Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i - 1}$ and height $\map f {x_i^*}$ with $x_i^* \in \closedint {x_{i - 1} } {x_i}$.

Their total area is the [[Definition:Riemann Sum|Riemann sum]]:
:$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {x_i^*} \Delta x_i$
By [[Continuous Real Function is Riemann Integrable]], these sums converge as $\norm P \to 0$.

The limit is $\displaystyle \int_a^b f$, which lies between the lower and upper sums bounding the region, and so equals the area under the curve.
{{qed}}
